doc.title: Robert Glasper interviewed by Greg Thomas, Clinton, New York, February 20, 2016

chapter: Black Radio and the new waves
title: Highlight of his career: the Black Radio Grammy and how it was made
summary: Winning the R&B Grammy was his peak; he describes the rushed Black Radio sessions, with guests like Ledisi.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Are we allowed to take photos or not?
Are we allowed to take any photos?
What’s the highlight of your career thus far? And is there another “Black Radio” coming or in the works?

The highlight of my career. I would probably say winning my first Grammy and it being an R&B Grammy. You know, for “Black Radio,” the original “Black Radio” album. I think that was the highlight pinnacle of my career because that’s like winning the NBA championship, you know, if you are a basketball player and you win the championship that’s the highlight of being a basketball player. You know. So for me that was one of the big moments. Because it was such a underdog kind of thing. You know what I mean? It was really like we went against the music industry, we went against radio, you know, we went against all the things that are supposed to work. I used — all the music was live. Couldn’t get all the people together in one room. And so I actually cancelled — I stopped the record. I didn’t even, I was like I can’t get everybody together and I was like forget it, let’s just go on tour. So we went on tour. And in the middle of my tour my manager just called me and said, “I don’t know how it’s happened but all these people, all 20 people, their managers called me and they’re all available this one week.” So and that was the next week. So I canceled my tour from Europe. I canceled the week and I flew to L.A. and that’s why there’s so many cover songs on “Black Radio” — we did like half of the record is cover songs. Because I didn’t have anything written because it was so last minute. You know what I mean? So I did a bunch of covers because I didn’t have any songs. And a lot of the songs we did were on the spot. The song we did with Ledisi, we re-did one of my old joints, “F.T.B.” because she literally came to the studio at three in the morning and we sat around a table and she was like, “what do you want to play?” You know, and I was like, “I don’t know, what do you want to do?” And we threw out some songs na, um, na, not that. I said, “this song?” She said, “okay, cool.” We listened to it, wrote lyrics to it, [claps] went in the studio. With King, they were a new group. You know, and My Home-Grown was managing them. And I went to their creative and I had to do my laundry, because I just got back from tour. They had a laundry. So I literally walked into the studio in the living room and I came up with this little idea and I was like, “here’s the idea. I’m gonna do my laundry.” So I did laundry. And I came back, the song was done. I was like, “great.” No this is literally how the album got done. So I always tell people the universe co-produces your album. You know what I mean? I mean I’ve learned that for a long time. The universe will co-produce your album and when things are not going right it may be for the better, but it’s hard to realize that in the moment. But it may take a left turn for something you didn’t know. Like the “Ah Yeah” song. “Ah Yeah” is probably the one song I would say catapulted my career from one to another.
